items.text: The system shall permit Autopilot operation only within a defined and validated operational design domain, and shall prevent or promptly end operation when road type, visibility, lane markings, or other conditions fall outside that domain.

The system shall continuously assess whether the driver is attentive and able to take control, using monitoring that does not rely solely on steering-wheel torque, and shall issue escalating warnings and take a defined safe action if the driver does not respond.

The system shall provide a safe fallback when it can no longer reliably control the vehicle, including when lane guidance or sensor inputs are lost or uncertain, and shall give the driver adequate warning and time to take control.

The system shall detect and respond safely to hazards in and near the vehicle’s path, including crossing or joining traffic, vehicles cutting in, large trucks, and motorcycles, rather than relying only on a vehicle identified in the same lane.

The system shall maintain a safe speed and following distance for current conditions, including road geometry, visibility, and traffic, and shall not accelerate when doing so would create an unsafe approach to a hazard.

The system shall monitor sensor and processing health, identify faults or disagreement between sensors, and prevent or limit automated control when the available information is insufficient for safe operation.

The system shall provide timely collision warnings and, when necessary, automatic braking for imminent collisions, with operation coordinated with Autopilot and not dependent on the driver noticing a warning.
The system shall clearly communicate to the driver whether Autopilot is available, active, limited, or disengaged, what functions it is controlling, and when the driver must take control.
The system shall ensure that any transfer of control to the driver is clear and predictable, and shall not disengage in a way that leaves the vehicle without adequate control or warning.
The system shall verify that lane-centering commands remain within safe limits and shall avoid steering toward detected obstacles or outside the drivable roadway when lane guidance is uncertain.

You are a requirements engineer reviewing a safety-critical system.

Read the system description below. List the 10 most important requirements that are missing from it:
things the system should do or guarantee for safe operation that the description does not cover.
Give at most 10, ranked from most to least important.

Reply with JSON only, in this shape:
{"requirements": [{"text": "The system shall ..."}]}

System description:
# Case: Tesla Model S with Autopilot (Williston, Florida, 2016)

Source: NTSB Highway Accident Report HAR-17/02. This is a description of the system and its use before the crash. It does not include the investigation findings.

## System
A 2015 Tesla Model S has Autopilot, a SAE Level 2 partial driving automation feature. It combines Traffic-Aware Cruise Control (TACC) and Autosteer (lane keeping). The driver stays responsible for driving and monitoring the road.

## Main parts
- Sensors: a forward-facing camera, a forward-facing radar and ultrasonic sensors.
- Vision processing: a camera-based system detects lane markings and objects ahead.
- TACC: holds a speed set by the driver, slows down for a vehicle ahead in the same lane, and speeds up again when the lane is clear.
- Autosteer: keeps the vehicle centered in its lane using lane markings and the vehicle ahead.
- Forward collision warning and automatic emergency braking are available as separate features.
- Driver monitoring: the system checks that the driver's hands are on the steering wheel by sensing steering torque, and shows visual and audible alerts if no hands are detected for a period of time.

## People
- The driver sets the cruising speed, turns Autopilot on, and is told to keep hands on the wheel and watch the road.
- Other road users include cars, large trucks crossing or joining the road, and motorcyclists.

## Operating context
Autopilot is intended mainly for highways with limited access, in good visibility. Drivers can also turn it on for other roads, such as divided highways with cross traffic at intersections.
